item.title: AI Spend Audit: How to Reduce Costs With Open Models
item.content:encoded:
AI Spend Audit: How to Reduce Costs With Open Models

Published on 2026.10.15 by Niklas

In 2026, mentions of open-weight or open-source models on US earnings calls and at investor conferences ran about six times higher compared to the last year. The companies doing the talking are no longer only tech firms. PNC, CH Robinson and Siemens have all discussed open-weight models in recent weeks.

The clearest example is Tinder. Its annualized AI spend climbed from roughly $1 million in January to roughly $10 million in July, and its CTO, Vinay Kuruvila, told the FT the company has started routing some queries from non-technical staff to open-weight models to bring costs under control. AT&T says open models already handle about 40% of its AI workload and that it wants to reach 70%, on a system that processes around 45 billion tokens a day. The FT also reports that open-weight models went from 7% of the tokens flowing through Vercel’s AI Gateway in December to 56% in August.

None of these companies announced that they left their frontier vendor. They did something less dramatic and more useful: they split their traffic. Simple, high-volume requests go to cheaper open models, and the work that genuinely needs a frontier model stays there. When “open-weight” starts appearing in CFO vocabulary, it means AI has stopped being an innovation line item and has become a cost line that someone has to explain.

This article covers how to find the movable workloads in your own request logs, how to price the move with real numbers, how to prove quality before you switch, and how to roll out without a bad week. The model comparisons use current list prices and independent benchmark data, and the worked example uses Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 as the baseline against DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Qwen3.8 Flash.

Start with the Bill Instead of the Model

Most teams begin an AI cost review by asking which model is best. That is the wrong first question. The right first question is which of your workloads are paying frontier prices for tasks that do not need frontier capability, and you cannot answer it without request-level data.

Pull a month of logs from your gateway, proxy or provider dashboards and make sure each call carries the following fields:

  • Application, team and feature (the business purpose, not just the API key)
  • Model and version
  • Input tokens, output tokens and cached tokens
  • Latency and retry count
  • Some signal of outcome, such as user acceptance, a downstream validation result or a thumbs rating
  • Cost per call

If you do not have feature-level tags today, add them before anything else. A week of tagged logs tells you more than a quarter of invoices. Once you have them, sort features by monthly spend and look at the top ten. That list is your audit scope. Everything below the top ten is rounding error until the big ones are handled.

Sort Workloads by How Bounded They Are

The single best predictor of whether a workload can move is how tightly bounded the task is. A task with a fixed output shape, a clear definition of correct, and a limited amount of reasoning is a strong candidate. A task that requires long chains of dependent decisions, or where a subtle mistake is expensive, is not.

Workload typeTypical profileMovability
Classification, routing, taggingFixed label set, short output, huge volumeHigh
Structured extractionKnown schema, programmatic validation possibleHigh
Summarization of tickets, calls, documentsBounded input, quality is forgivingHigh
Retrieval-based Q&A over internal docsAnswers are grounded in supplied contextMedium to high
Support and sales drafting with human reviewA person catches the missesMedium to high
Code boilerplate, tests, documentationVerifiable by running itMedium
Multi-step agentic coding, long-horizon tool useErrors compound across stepsLow, keep on frontier
High-stakes judgment (regulated, legal, medical)Cost of a wrong answer is largeEvaluate heavily before moving

You do not have to guess at where the capability gap lives. Public benchmark data for Claude Opus 5.5 versus DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, drawn from the Vals AI benchmark suite as of late September, shows that the gap is far from uniform. On the aggregate Vals Index, Opus 5.5 scores 69.7 and V4.1 Flash scores 57.9, so Flash lands at roughly 83% of the flagship overall. The task-level picture matters more than that single number.

BenchmarkClaude Opus 5.5DeepSeek V4.1 FlashGap
MedScribe (clinical note generation)91.4%85.5%Small
Vibe Code Bench v1.190.3%84.7%Small
Public Benefits Bench70.6%64.3%Small
Tax Agent Bench70.5%62.5%Moderate
Terminal-Bench 2.187.6%74.5%Moderate
CyberBench v1.155.4%73.7%Flash ahead
ProofBench100%54%Large
IOI (competitive programming)95.1%40.3%Large
Terminal-Bench 4.061.6%11.6%Very large
SRE Bench33.6%0.8%Very large

The pattern is consistent with the table above it. Bounded professional tasks (documentation, structured analysis, code generation that can be tested) sit within single digits of the flagship. Long-horizon agent work and competition-grade reasoning is where the open model falls away. This is why the audit is a workload exercise and not a vendor decision. The same model can be an easy yes for your ticket summarizer and a clear no for your autonomous incident-response agent.

Price the Move with Real Numbers

Here are the list prices that matter for this comparison, per million tokens. DeepInfra rates for the two open models are as tracked on OpenRouter and public price trackers in early October 2026, and they change often, so check current rates before you build a business case.

ModelInputOutputLicense
Claude Opus 5.5$4.00$20.00Proprietary
Claude Sonnet 5.5$2.00$10.00Proprietary
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (DeepInfra)$0.14$0.42Open weights
Qwen3.8 Flash (DeepInfra)$0.113$0.382Open weights

Per-token prices are not a business case on their own, so take a concrete workload. Imagine a feature that handles 1 million requests a month, each averaging 3,000 input tokens (a prompt, some retrieved context, an instruction) and 500 output tokens. That is 3 billion input tokens and 500 million output tokens monthly.

ModelMonthly costAnnual costMultiple vs. Opus 5.5
Claude Opus 5.5$22,000$264,0001x
Claude Sonnet 5.5$11,000$132,0002x cheaper
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash$630$7,56035x cheaper
Qwen3.8 Flash$530$6,36042x cheaper

Against a Sonnet baseline the gap is smaller but still large: Qwen3.8 Flash comes in about 21x cheaper and V4.1 Flash about 17.5x cheaper at list price

Those multiples are the ceiling, not the forecast. Three things pull the real number down, and an honest business case accounts for each.

  • Verbosity: Reasoning-heavy open models can generate far more output tokens per task than a flagship tuned for concision. Artificial Analysis found that the first DeepSeek V4 models produced several times the median token volume on its Intelligence Index. Measure tokens per completed task on your own workload, not just price per token. Independent cost-per-task figures are a better guide than list prices: at V4 Flash’s launch, Artificial Analysis estimated an average cost of about 3 cents per benchmark task, against $3.15 for Claude Fable 5. That is still roughly 100x, but it is a very different statement from comparing rate cards.
  • Tokenization: Different model families split the same text into different numbers of tokens, and Anthropic has noted that its recent tokenizers produce meaningfully more tokens for the same text than older ones. Compare cost per task rather than cost per million tokens.
  • Fallbacks: No cheap model clears every request. The realistic design is a tiered one, where the cheap model answers first and the hard cases escalate to the frontier model. The cost of that escalation belongs in the model. Here is the same workload with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash as the first tier and Opus 5.5 as the fallback.
Escalation rate to Opus 5.5Monthly costMultiple vs. all-Opus
0%$63035x
2%$1,07021x
4%$1,51015x
10%$2,8308x
20%$5,0304x

At a 4% escalation rate, the tiered design runs at about 15x cheaper than all-Opus, which comes to roughly $245,000 saved per year on this single feature. If Flash also emits double the output tokens, that same 4% scenario lands near 13x. The savings are real and large, and they are very sensitive to how often the cheap model needs help. That sensitivity is precisely why the next two steps exist.

One more fairness note for finance readers. The baseline has been moving too. Opus 5.5 launched at $4 and $20 per million tokens, down from $5 and $25 for Opus 5, and Anthropic says its tests show about 40% lower cost per task on typical workloads because the model uses fewer tokens. Price your current model at today’s rates, with your real cache-hit rate, since cached input on Opus 5.5 is $0.20 per million. A stale baseline will overstate your savings and cost you credibility with the CFO.

Prove Quality on Your Own Traffic

Public benchmarks tell you where to look. Your own logs tell you whether the move is safe. Build a small evaluation for each candidate workload before any traffic shifts.

  • Sample real requests. Pull 500 to 1,000 production requests per workload, stratified across the input types you see (short and long, easy and awkward, every language you support). Freeze this set. It becomes your regression suite for every future model change.
  • Capture the baseline. Run the set through the incumbent model and store the outputs along with any known outcomes, such as what the user accepted or what the downstream system did with the result.
  • Grade with the cheapest reliable method. For structured tasks, use programmatic checks: schema validity, exact-match on key fields, unit tests for generated code. For open-ended tasks, use an LLM judge, but calibrate it first by having humans grade a subset of 100 or so items and checking that the judge agrees with them. For high-stakes workloads, keep human review in the loop.
  • Write the acceptance bar before you look at results. For example: at least 97% of baseline task success, no increase in severe errors, format validity above 99%, and tokens per task within an agreed multiple of the baseline. Teams that set the bar after seeing the numbers tend to move it.
  • Look at the tail, not the average. An average quality score of 97% can hide a cluster of failures on one customer segment or one document type. Slice results by input category and read the worst fifty outputs by hand.

Then run the candidate in shadow mode: production traffic goes to both models, users only see the incumbent’s answer, and you compare. Shadow mode costs a little extra for a couple of weeks and removes most of the guesswork.

Roll Out with a Safety Net

Once a workload clears the bar, the rollout should be boring. The design that most enterprise teams converge on has five parts.

Cheap model first, frontier on escalation

Define explicit triggers: output fails schema validation, a confidence score falls below a threshold, the request matches a risk category, or the user asks again. Small decision models, which return a choice and a calibrated confidence score without generating text, are well suited to the routing step because they add very little latency and cost.

Canary the traffic

Start at 5% of a single workload, hold for several days, then move to 25%, then 100%. Keep the old path warm until the new one has survived a full business cycle, including month-end or any other seasonal peak.

Keep a kill switch

Every routed workload needs a one-line configuration change that sends 100% of traffic back to the incumbent. Test it before you need it.

Monitor what finance and engineering care about

Track escalation rate, task success rate, severe-error rate and tokens per task alongside cost per accepted task. A rising escalation rate is the early warning that your savings are eroding.

Pin versions and re-run the suite

Open-weight providers release updates quickly, and some releases are previews whose behavior can shift between versions. Pin model versions in production and re-run your frozen evaluation set before adopting any new one.

Running the Cheap Tier on DeepInfra

DeepInfra serves open models through an OpenAI-compatible API, so adding a cheap tier to an existing pipeline means pointing a second client at a different base URL. Here is a minimal tiered pattern with schema validation and an escalation path.

import json
from openai import OpenAI

cheap = OpenAI(
    api_key="YOUR_DEEPINFRA_API_KEY",
    base_url="https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai",
)

CHEAP_MODEL = "deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash"  

def is_valid(text: str) -> bool:
    try:
        data = json.loads(text)
        return {"category", "priority"} <= data.keys()
    except (ValueError, AttributeError):
        return False

def classify_ticket(ticket: str) -> str:
    response = cheap.chat.completions.create(
        model=CHEAP_MODEL,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": "Return JSON with category and priority."},
            {"role": "user", "content": ticket},
        ],
        temperature=0,
    )
    answer = response.choices[0].message.content

    if is_valid(answer):
        return answer          # cheap tier handled it

    return call_frontier(ticket)  # your existing incumbent clientcopy

The validation function is where your escalation rate is decided. Log every escalation with the reason, and review them weekly, because that log tells you exactly which requests the cheap tier cannot handle and whether the threshold needs adjusting.

The Bottom Line

The shift the Financial Times describes is not a story about companies abandoning frontier models. It is a story about companies discovering that a large share of their AI traffic never needed one. At list prices, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Qwen3.8 Flash cost between roughly 17x and 42x less than Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 on a typical workload. After verbosity and fallback costs, a realistic planning number for a well-chosen workload is closer to 10x to 15x. That is still the difference between a six-figure line item and a five-figure one for a single feature.

The gap in capability is real and uneven. It is small on bounded professional tasks and very large on long-horizon agent work, so the audit has to be done workload by workload, with your own logs and your own acceptance bar. Teams that do that work end up with a routing layer, a frozen evaluation suite and a cost-per-accepted-task metric that finance trusts. Those three assets matter more than any one model choice, because they let you take advantage of the next price drop in an afternoon instead of a quarter.

Built for agents and pipelines that need to execute untrusted code without you having to run the infrastructure yourself.

It handles text input and output across a 1,048,576-token context window, and is one of several hundred models in DeepInfra’s catalog. The model uses the same base as GLM-5.2. Every gain comes from post-training, which is where Z.ai […]</p>

As a 2.8-trillion-parameter native multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model, Kimi K3 is engineered to handle demanding computational tasks, from complex software engineering and long-horizon agentic workflows to deep scientific research. item.description: Full title: From Screenshots to Tool Calls: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on DeepInfra
item.content:encoded:
From Screenshots to Tool Calls: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on DeepInfra

Published on 2026.10.15 by Aray Sultanbekova

NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, the new open multimodal model in the Nemotron family, is available on DeepInfra from day zero. Starting today, you can call it through our OpenAI-compatible API with no deployment setup and pay-per-token pricing.

Agents are moving past text. A support agent has to read the screenshot a customer pasted. A finance workflow has to pull line items from a scanned invoice. A research agent has to make sense of the chart on page 14.

One way to build these workflows is to put an OCR or vision model in front of a separate reasoning model. That works, but it adds another handoff, another integration, and another place where useful content can get lost.

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL brings visual understanding and reasoning together in one model, making it easier to build agents that work with what they see.

What makes Nemotron 3.5 Super VL different?

Super VL joins the Nemotron family alongside Nemotron 3.5 Lightning for efficient, high-volume text workloads and Nemotron 3 Ultra for complex reasoning and planning. Super VL is the choice when your workflow needs visual understanding alongside reasoning and tool use.

Visual understanding and tool use. Super VL works with text, images, documents, and application screenshots, using visual context to reason about the next step and generate tool calls.

One model for seeing and acting. Most visual pipelines split perception from reasoning. Super VL reads the document or screenshot and then decides which tool to call, keeping the task in one context instead of passing summaries between models.

Large-model capacity, small-model compute. Its Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture has approximately 121B parameters, 12.7B active per token. Each mixture-of-experts layer routes a token to 22 of its 512 routed experts, plus a shared expert. This provides the capacity of a large model with a much smaller active compute footprint.

Built for long agent loops. The backbone combines Mamba-2, mixture-of-experts, and attention layers. Only 8 of its 88 layers use attention. Mamba layers carry a fixed-size state instead of a cache that grows with every token, helping long conversations and multi-page documents remain efficient. On DeepInfra, the model has a 262K-token context window, giving applications room to work with long documents and multi-turn conversations.

Fast by design. A built-in multi-token prediction (MTP) head drafts several tokens per step. With NVFP4 weights on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, DeepInfra reports generation speed above 400 tokens per second in its tested single-request configuration.

Benchmarking done in collaboration with the Artificial Analysis team.

Open and customizable. The weights are open, and NVIDIA publishes NeMo recipes for fine-tuning and LoRA on your own data, tools, and policies. This provides a path to higher accuracy on specialized multimodal tasks.

The model understands 10 languages: English, French, Spanish, Italian, German, Japanese, Hindi, Korean, Brazilian Portuguese, and Chinese.

What you can build

  • Document intelligence: Extract fields, tables, and chart values from PDFs, scans, and complex layouts across many pages, then generate summaries or reports. For structured workflows, Super VL can return extracted information as schema-constrained JSON.
  • Customer service agents: Resolve multi-step requests by reading the documents and screenshots customers send, applying policy, and calling service tools.
  • Computer-use and GUI agents: Understand application screens, dashboards, and forms, then decide on the next action.
  • Multimodal research agents: Combine information found in charts and documents with results from search and retrieval tools.

Getting started on DeepInfra

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL works with any OpenAI-compatible client. Get an API key from the DeepInfra dashboard, set it as DEEPINFRA_TOKEN, and point the client at the DeepInfra endpoint.

The example below gives the model a screenshot of a customer's order page. The model identifies the order number and calls a function that can retrieve the latest shipping information.

import base64
import os

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["DEEPINFRA_TOKEN"],
    base_url="https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai",
)

MODEL = "nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL"

tools = [
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "lookup_order",
            "description": "Look up an order by ID and return its shipping status.",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {"order_id": {"type": "string"}},
                "required": ["order_id"],
            },
        },
    }
]

with open("screenshot.png", "rb") as f:
    screenshot_b64 = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode()

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model=MODEL,
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": f"data:image/png;base64,{screenshot_b64}"}},
                {"type": "text", "text": "A customer sent this screenshot. Find their order and tell me if it has shipped."},
            ],
        }
    ],
    tools=tools,
)

message = response.choices[0].message
for call in message.tool_calls:
    print(call.function.name, call.function.arguments)

# The model's reasoning is returned alongside the tool call
print(message.reasoning_content)

Input: the customer's screenshot.

Output (0.5 s, finish_reason: tool_calls):

lookup_order {"order_id": "SL-48213-77"}

# the model's reasoning, abridged
The status shown in the image is "Preparing
to ship", but I should verify this using the
lookup_order function to get the most accurate
and current information.

Notice that it didn't just read the status badge off the screen. It recognized that a screenshot can be stale and went to the source of truth.

item.title: Western Open-Weight Models: Beam and Le Chonk
item.content:encoded:
Western Open-Weight Models: Beam and Le Chonk

Published on 2026.10.14 by Stefan Fidanov

Reflection AI and Mistral shipped open-weight flagships a day apart in the first week of October, and both say they compare to the best China has to offer.

Reflection’s Beam is a 501B-parameter workhorse that claims GLM-5.2-level reasoning, a bar Z.ai has already raised with GLM-5.3, on a fraction of the inference compute. Mistral’s Large 4, which the company nicknamed “le Chonk,” is a 1-trillion-parameter flagship built, trained, and served in Europe.

Chinese labs still set the bar on price per capability, and neither launch moves it. On Artificial Analysis’s open-weights index, Le Chonk scores 38 against 46 for MiMo-V2.6-Pro and 45 for GLM-5.3.

So the Western pitch rests on four other questions: where the model runs, who operates it, which license applies, and what each answer costs. Let’s explore this in more detail.

At A Glance: Beam, Le Chonk, And The Bar They’re Chasing

Here’s each launch next to its named Chinese rivals and the strongest US open model in production. Beam and Le Chonk rows are launch-day promises.

ModelOriginTotal / active paramsLicenseWeightsWhere you can run it today (prices: DeepInfra)
Reflection BeamUS501B / 23BApache 2.0 (promised)“Later this month”Waitlist API at Reflection
Mistral Large 4 (le Chonk)France1.05T / 49BNot yet namedEnd of OctoberMistral Studio preview, $1.36 / $4.18 per 1M
GLM-5.3China753B / ~40BCustom GLM-5.3 LicensePublicDeepInfra, $0.90 / $4.00 per 1M
Kimi K3China2.8T / 104BKimi K3 LicensePublicDeepInfra, $2.85 / $14.25 per 1M
DeepSeek V4.1 FlashChina552B / 16BMITPublicDeepInfra, $0.20 / $0.60 per 1M
InklingUS975B / 41BApache 2.0PublicDeepInfra, $0.95 / $4.05 per 1M

The Price-Per-Capability Bar Chinese Labs Set

For the last year and a half, the open-weight frontier has been Chinese. Nathan Lambert’s Interconnects dates the clear Chinese lead to around April 2025, and Hugging Face’s summer 2026 state of open models found that this year’s releases above 100B parameters were built on Chinese models or used Chinese-lab artifacts.

Chinese labs also paired strong models with aggressive pricing. On Artificial Analysis’s open-weights leaderboard (Intelligence Index v4.3.2), MiMo-V2.6-Pro scores 46, GLM-5.3 scores 45, Kimi K3 scores 44, and GLM-5.3-Flash scores 42. The best US entries on that leaderboard are Inkling at 25 and Nemotron 3 Ultra at 23. Le Chonk lands at 38 on its own Artificial Analysis page, and AA’s launch analysis calls it the “most intelligent model from outside the US and China.”

Here they are against output price.

The upper-left corner belongs to China. GLM-5.3-Flash scores 42 at $0.50 per million output tokens on DeepInfra, and the Western models score lower at higher prices. Beam is missing because it has no data on either axis yet. Artificial Analysis hasn’t scored it, and Reflection hasn’t published pricing. On benchmark per dollar alone, it’s easy to see why both labs chose to argue about something else. (We covered the broader open vs closed version of this trade-off separately.)

Beam: A Workhorse Sold On Compute Per Answer

Reflection’s launch post concedes that Kimi K3 remains ahead on raw capability, so it sells Beam on efficiency instead. Beam, it says, “achieves scores comparable to GLM-5.2 while using 3–4× less inference compute.” Beam is a text-only mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 501B total parameters and 23B active per token, pretrained on 23.8T tokens across 6,144 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs.

Read the footnote before you quote that number. Reflection defines generation compute as roughly 2 × active parameters × mean generated tokens per attempt, counting reasoning plus the final answer. That makes it an estimate, and its first factor is easy to chart:

Beam’s 23B active parameters (highlighted) against GLM-5.2’s roughly 40B give it about a 1.7x edge per token. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash are leaner still. To reach 3-4x, the remainder has to come from Beam generating fewer tokens per answer. Artificial Analysis, which had early access, said Beam looks like “one of the most token-efficient open models we’ve seen for its level of intelligence.” Here’s the arithmetic:

def decode_flops(active_params_b: float, generated_tokens: int) -> float:
    """Reflection's proxy: 2 x active params x generated tokens (decode only)."""
    return 2 * active_params_b * 1e9 * generated_tokens

# Active parameters, in billions
BEAM, GLM_5_2 = 23, 40

param_ratio = GLM_5_2 / BEAM
print(f"Per-token advantage from active params: {param_ratio:.2f}x")

# What token ratio would close the gap to Reflection's 3-4x claim?
for claimed in (3.0, 4.0):
    implied = claimed / param_ratio
    print(f"{claimed:.0f}x total implies GLM-5.2 writes {implied:.2f}x more tokens per answer")

# Sanity check with a hypothetical 6,000-token reasoning trace
print(f"Beam, 6k tokens: {decode_flops(BEAM, 6_000) / 1e12:.0f} TFLOPs")copy

So GLM-5.2 would need to write roughly 1.7x to 2.3x more output tokens for the same result. Does Beam actually reason that briefly? That’s unverified until the weights ship and independent evaluators measure its output length. Once it’s callable, test the claim on your own prompts. The formula also leaves out the costs that dominate agent workloads.

Prefill is the big one. An agent loop that re-reads a 100K-token context on every tool call spends most of its compute reading, and the 3-4x number says nothing about that phase. All 501B parameters also have to sit in GPU memory even though only 23B fire per token. Cost per finished task tracks turns and tokens more than per-token price, as we argued in small open-weight models’ hidden cost advantage.

Le Chonk: A Flagship Sold On Where It Runs

Mistral went the other way. Mistral Large 4 is a 1.05T-parameter MoE with 49B active per token (52B if you count embeddings and output layers, per its Hugging Face card). It takes text and image input across more than 160 languages, and Mistral says it significantly outperforms “any open-weight model developed in the US or Europe.” On specs, plan around what is served, not what is printed: Mistral’s docs list a 1M-token context window, but Artificial Analysis lists roughly 512K for the preview API it tested, and Beam’s beta API caps requests at 256K against a claimed 1M.

The headline is jurisdiction. Mistral says Large 4 was trained from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in its own European datacenters, and the preview is served on the same hardware. It will run in “a European deployment that Mistral operates end-to-end, independently of other digital service providers and under European law,” and for security work it can run on private cloud or on-premise. Guillaume Lample put the reasoning bluntly to WIRED: “If you use a closed model, there is no guarantee it will still be there tomorrow.”

Think of it as a ladder, where each rung moves the model closer to hardware you control.

Today Le Chonk sits on the bottom two rungs, and the top two depend on a license Mistral hasn’t named. The capability is real but . Artificial Analysis measured $1.13 per Intelligence Index task at list price, more than 4x what higher-scored open models like GLM-5.3-Flash cost, partly because Large 4 produced 200M output tokens to finish the index against a median of 82M. The data sovereignty case for open weights only pays off once you can actually climb the ladder. Both launches also lack independent serving numbers. No measured latency, throughput, or time to first token under load exists for Beam or Large 4, so the ladder assesses where a model can run; how well it serves stays unknown until weights ship and providers publish measurements.

Reading The Scoreboard

Both launch posts carry vendor-reported benchmarks. Reflection’s is more complete, and it includes competitors its headline skips. Below is a subset of Reflection’s published numbers as of October 8 (Beam’s scores were revised that day). Competitor scores are Reflection’s compilation from third-party leaderboards, so read the table as claimed scores against the baselines Reflection chose. Bold marks the row leader, and NR means not reported.

BenchmarkBeamInklingNemotron 3 UltraGLM-5.2GLM-5.3Kimi K3DeepSeek V4.1 Flash
Terminal Bench v2.180.163.856.481.088.288.390.6
DeepSWE v1.144.4NRNR44.061.068.074.2
SWE Bench Pro v165.554.346.462.1NRNRNR
HLE (no tools)36.229.726.740.542.346.939.1
GPQA Diamond90.587.287.091.291.793.590.9
MCP Atlas78.776.063.177.884.282.3NR

Source: reflection.ai/beam, all scores vendor-reported.

Within that chosen set, Beam beats the two US models, Inkling and Nemotron 3 Ultra, on every shared row, and those are also the table’s two weakest models. GLM-5.2, the model in Reflection’s headline, is no longer Z.ai’s flagship. GLM-5.3 shipped in late August and leads Beam on every row where both report. Mistral reports Large 4 at 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, level with the 61.0 Reflection’s table prints for GLM-5.3, but VentureBeat points out that the live leaderboard has Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3 nearer 69%. Treat both vendors’ tables as dated snapshots of a moving leaderboard. For more on the Chinese side, see our Kimi K3 vs DeepSeek V4 Pro vs GLM-5.2 comparison.

Le Chonk’s numbers live on a different scoreboard, since what exists for it is Mistral’s own claims plus Artificial Analysis’s independent measurements:

Le Chonk measureValue
Intelligence Index v4.3.238
DeepSWE v1.1 (Mistral-reported)61.7%
DeepSWE v1.1 (live leaderboard: Kimi K3, GLM-5.3)~69%
Cost per Index task at list price$1.13
Output tokens to finish the Index200M (median model: 82M)

Sources: Artificial Analysis’s model page and launch analysis, Mistral’s launch post, VentureBeat. Read the two tables together and the picture is the same from both launches: neither Western flagship beats GLM-5.3 on a scale anyone else can check.

The Rest Of The Western Open-Weight Bench

Several other Western options are deployable today. None matches GLM-5.3 on capability, but several win on license and price.

ModelLabTotal / activeLicenseAA Index v4.3.2DeepInfra $/1M in / outBest role
InklingThinking Machines (US)975B / 41BApache 2.025$0.95 / $4.05Multimodal agents (text, image, audio in)
Nemotron 3 UltraNVIDIA (US)550B / 55BOpenMDW 1.123$0.50 / $2.20Reasoning where open data and recipe matter
Nemotron 3 SuperNVIDIA (US)120B / 12BNVIDIA Nemotron Open Model LicenseNot listed$0.085 / $0.40Cheap agent steps
gpt-oss-120bOpenAI (US)117B / 5.1BApache 2.0Not listed$0.037 / $0.17Classification, routing, bulk extraction
Gemma 4 31BGoogle (US)31B denseApache 2.0Not listed$0.20 / $0.40Small-footprint self-hosting

Inkling is the closest thing to a Western Beam that you can call right now. It’s a 975B MoE under Apache 2.0, and it accepts audio, which neither Beam nor Le Chonk does. Nemotron 3 Ultra’s selling point is openness beyond the weights, since NVIDIA released training data and recipes alongside the checkpoints. At the cheap end, gpt-oss-120b and Nemotron 3 Super are the grunt-work picks. At $0.17 and $0.40 per million output tokens, frontier capability stops mattering for triage and routing steps.

Licensing Is Where Western Open-Weight Models Can Win

Scan the license columns and the Chinese flagships are drifting toward custom terms. GLM-5.2 shipped under plain MIT, but GLM-5.3 moved to its own license, which requires companies above $10B in revenue to pass Z.ai’s security review before offering it as a hosted service. Kimi K3 and Qwen3.8-Max ship under their own named licenses with commercial conditions. DeepSeek is the holdout, still on MIT.

The Western side is moving the other way, at least at Reflection. Beam’s weights are promised under Apache 2.0, which matches Inkling, gpt-oss-120b, and Gemma 4. That’s the license legal teams approve without a meeting. Mistral is the open question. Its previous flagship, Mistral Large 3, was Apache 2.0, but its most recent mid-size release, Medium 3.5, uses a modified MIT license that excludes companies with more than $20M in monthly revenue. Large 4’s Hugging Face page has no license field at all.

Axios also notes that the FY2026 NDAA directs the Defense Department to remove DeepSeek from government and contractor systems, and that Western releases give businesses alternatives to Chinese options they may have eschewed for security reasons. Reflection CEO Misha Laskin told Axios: “Once you’re spending that amount on intelligence, you want to move from renting it to owning it yourself.”

Three different risks hide inside the word “origin”.

  • Serving location is whose datacenter processes your prompts: every model you can call on DeepInfra today, Chinese-origin or not, runs in US data centers with zero retention, which covers most data-handling concerns.
  • Weights origin is who built the model and what its license permits, which drives legal exposure and what you can change.
  • Statutory procurement is the narrowest case and the only one where origin is disqualifying by itself: if the NDAA or a customer contract excludes Chinese-origin weights, no amount of US serving changes that, and Beam, Le Chonk, Inkling, Nemotron, and gpt-oss are your choices.

If statutory procurement isn’t your situation, the Chinese flagships earn their place on price per capability. The same split answers the obvious question about Le Chonk: if you need it under European law specifically, that path runs through Mistral’s own EU deployment or self-hosting once the weights ship; a US inference provider can’t offer European jurisdiction.

Running Western Open-Weight Models On Deepinfra Today

You don’t need to wait for either launch to build the plumbing. Make model choice a policy decision in code, so origin and license sit next to price in one place. DeepInfra serves a huge collection of models through one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so the policy is just a list of model IDs.

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["DEEPINFRA_API_TOKEN"],
    base_url="https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai",
)

# Candidates per role, tagged with origin and license.
# Add Beam or Mistral Large 4 here once a provider serves their weights.
CATALOG = {
    "agent": [
        ("thinkingmachines/Inkling", "US", "apache-2.0"),
        ("nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B", "US", "openmdw-1.1"),
        ("zai-org/GLM-5.3", "CN", "glm-5.3"),
    ],
    "triage": [
        ("openai/gpt-oss-120b", "US", "apache-2.0"),
        ("deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash", "CN", "mit"),
    ],
}

POLICY = {"origins": {"US", "EU"}, "licenses": {"apache-2.0", "openmdw-1.1", "mit"}}


def allowed(role: str) -> list[str]:
    return [
        model for model, origin, license_id in CATALOG[role]
        if origin in POLICY["origins"] and license_id in POLICY["licenses"]
    ]


def complete(role: str, messages: list[dict]) -> str:
    last_error = None
    for model in allowed(role):  # first allowed model wins, the rest are fallbacks
        try:
            resp = client.chat.completions.create(model=model, messages=messages, timeout=60)
            return resp.choices[0].message.content
        except Exception as err:
            last_error = err
    raise RuntimeError(f"No allowed model succeeded for role {role!r}") from last_error


print(complete("triage", [{"role": "user", "content": "Classify: 'refund not received'"}]))copy

Loosen POLICY and GLM-5.3 joins the agent pool. When Beam’s weights land, it’s one more tuple.

Next, build a token-efficiency check, since Beam’s argument rests on generated tokens per answer. Run one prompt set across candidates and record what each wrote:

import asyncio
import os
from openai import AsyncOpenAI

client = AsyncOpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["DEEPINFRA_API_TOKEN"],
    base_url="https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai",
)

# (model id, active params in billions, $ per 1M input, $ per 1M output)
CANDIDATES = [
    ("thinkingmachines/Inkling", 41, 0.95, 4.05),
    ("nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B", 55, 0.50, 2.20),
    ("zai-org/GLM-5.3", 40, 0.90, 4.00),
]

PROMPT = [{"role": "user", "content": "Find the bug: def avg(xs): return sum(xs) / len(xs) - 1"}]


async def measure(model: str, active_b: float, price_in: float, price_out: float) -> dict:
    resp = await client.chat.completions.create(model=model, messages=PROMPT)
    u = resp.usage
    return {
        "model": model.split("/")[-1],
        "out_tokens": u.completion_tokens,
        "decode_tflops": 2 * active_b * 1e9 * u.completion_tokens / 1e12,
        "cost_usd": (u.prompt_tokens * price_in + u.completion_tokens * price_out) / 1e6,
    }


async def main():
    rows = await asyncio.gather(*(measure(*c) for c in CANDIDATES))
    for r in sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r["cost_usd"]):
        print(f"{r['model']:<40} {r['out_tokens']:>6} tok  {r['decode_tflops']:>7.1f} TFLOPs  ${r['cost_usd']:.5f}")


asyncio.run(main())copy

Run it over a few hundred real prompts and you get Reflection’s proxy, measured on your workload. When Beam is callable, add a row and see whether the 3-4x survives contact with your traffic.

Everything here runs on DeepInfra’s pay-as-you-go pricing with no contract, on zero-retention US infrastructure with SOC 2 and ISO 27001 certification.

Conclusion

Neither Beam nor Le Chonk closes the gap with the best Chinese open models. Reflection’s own table shows that, and so does Artificial Analysis. They change the terms of the comparison instead. The split is almost tidy: Beam, sold on writing fewer tokens per answer, argues compute per answer and an Apache 2.0 license, while Le Chonk, which burned 200M output tokens finishing Artificial Analysis’s index, argues European operation and on-prem control. Inkling, the Nemotron 3 models, and gpt-oss-120b are already competing on permissive licensing and price. If your procurement rules exclude Chinese-origin weights, that’s a real menu for the first time, and it grows when the weights land.

Start with the models you can run today on DeepInfra’s model catalog, wire up the routing policy, and the new Western open-weight models become one-line additions. Questions about any of these models? Reach us at feedback@deepinfra.com, join our Discord, or find us on X at @DeepInfra.

FAQ

Is Reflection Beam available on DeepInfra?

Not yet. As of launch, Beam was available only through a waitlist beta on Reflection’s own OpenAI-compatible API, and its Hugging Face organization had no public models. Reflection has promised Apache 2.0 weights later in October, and inference providers can host the model once those ship. Until then, the closest Western MoE on DeepInfra is Inkling.

When will Mistral Large 4 weights be released, and under what license?

Mistral says by the end of October, and its Hugging Face page lists an October 31 ETA. Mistral hasn’t announced a license, and its recent releases don’t settle the question, so check the LICENSE file before planning a self-hosted deployment.

Is Beam actually 3-4x cheaper to run than GLM-5.2?

Not necessarily in dollars. The 3-4x figure estimates decode compute alone, and Reflection hasn’t published pricing, so dollar cost is unknown. The token-efficiency check in the code section above measures it on your traffic.

item.title: Decision Models: The Fast Layer for AI Agents
item.content:encoded:
Decision Models: The Fast Layer for AI Agents

Published on 2026.10.13 by Niklas

There is a decision your agent makes dozens of times per session that you are probably paying a frontier model to handle. Should this request go to the fast cheap model or the expensive one? Is this tool call safe to execute? Is the task actually finished, or does the agent think it is finished? Which of these six retrieved documents is relevant to the question?

Every one of those is a bounded choice with a fixed option set. None of them requires generating prose. None of them requires chain-of-thought. None of them should cost what a Claude or GPT-5.5 call costs. But for most teams building agent pipelines today, that is exactly what they are paying because the LLM already in the loop is the path of least resistance for any decision that cannot be handled by a rules table.

A new model category arrived in September 2026 to solve this problem, and it spread faster than anything in the agent tooling space in the past year. TypeSafe AI released Jev on September 15. Laya, an open-source alternative, followed three days later. Kev, an open decoder-based implementation, appeared in the same week. AWS released Strands Decider 2B on October 1. OpenAI announced the Decisions API at DevDay 2026 the same week and moved it to public beta on October 6. A local runtime called Ollaya appeared shortly after, bundling seven open decision models behind a single API endpoint. The category went from nonexistent to contested in under three weeks.

This article explains what a decision model actually is, how the architecture differs from a generative LLM, what the current landscape looks like across proprietary and open options, where these models fit in an agent pipeline, and what the honest limitations are.

What a Decision Model Actually Is

A decision model takes two inputs: a block of context (a message, a document, an agent’s conversation history, a tool call’s proposed parameters) and a set of predefined possible answers. It returns one answer from that set, plus a confidence score for each option. It never generates text. The output is always one of the choices you supplied, with a probability attached.

TypeSafe calls this a “System One model” which is a deliberate reference to Kahneman’s dual-process framework, positioning decision models as the fast, automatic cognition layer that handles bounded judgments while the generative LLM handles the slow, deliberate reasoning.

The name has stuck across the field even for non-TypeSafe implementations. Three question types have become the standard interface across all implementations in this space:

Question typeReturnsExample
ChoiceOne option from a fixed listRoute this ticket: billing / technical / shipping / other
ScoreA number between 0 and 1Urgency score from 0 (low) to 1 (critical)
Noul (yes/no)A probability between 0 and 1Is this tool call grounded in what the user said?

The confidence score is not a courtesy feature. It is the mechanism that makes decision models automatable. A generative LLM asked to classify a message as billing or technical will almost always give you an answer even when the message is genuinely ambiguous because that is what text generation does. A decision model with calibrated confidence scores lets you set a threshold: auto-act above 0.85, escalate to a human or a bigger model below it. You can tune where that threshold sits based on the cost of a wrong decision in your specific context. That is not something you can do cleanly with a generative model’s output.

How the Architecture Works

The defining architectural characteristic of a decision model is that it does not have a language modeling head. A standard transformer-based LLM ends with a head that produces a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary at every generation step, and then samples from that distribution sequentially to produce text. That vocabulary projection is expensive, and sequential sampling is why text generation takes seconds.

A decision model removes the vocabulary head and replaces it with a pointer head or decision head that scores only the specific options you supplied. There is no vocabulary. There is no sampling. The model reads the context, reads the options, and produces a score for each option in a single forward pass.

This architectural difference produces a dramatic latency reduction. Jev reports 70–500ms end-to-end latency versus 3+ seconds for frontier models. OpenAI’s Decisions API demonstrated roughly 150ms versus 1,600ms for standard Luna calls at DevDay which is approximately 10x faster. AWS Strands Decider 2B running on an H100 GPU reports sub-100ms decision time.

The other consequence of removing the vocabulary head is that there is no output token cost. Decision models charge for input only. At $0.042/M input tokens for Jev, the cost comparison versus a frontier model call is not marginal. A pipeline routing 10 million decisions per month through Jev spends $420. The same decisions through Claude Haiku 4.5, which is already one of the cheaper generative options, costs orders of magnitude more once you factor in the output tokens required to express the classification.

How Each Model Trains Calibration

The confidence scores a decision model returns are only useful if they are calibrated and a 0.85 confidence actually corresponds to being right 85% of the time. Getting calibration right is harder than getting accuracy right, and it is where the different models in this category diverge technically.

The training approach that has become standard across all serious implementations is called RLCD: Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions. Rather than training on cross-entropy loss (which optimizes for accuracy but produces overconfident outputs), RLCD trains the model to maximize strictly proper scoring rules. The Brier score and logarithmic scoring rules are the most common. A model trained this way has an incentive to say 0.6 when it is genuinely 60% confident, rather than rounding up to 0.95 to collect a slightly higher accuracy reward.

Laya documents its RLCD implementation publicly: GRPO-style policy gradient with a combination of logarithmic, spherical, and ranked probability scoring rules as the reward, with no supervised cross-entropy loss at all. TypeSafe describes Jev as trained with RLCD but does not publish the details. Strands Decider 2B’s training recipe, published with the model weights under Apache 2.0, describes a similar approach.

The practical consequence of calibration quality shows up in threshold-based routing. If your decision model consistently returns 0.92 confidence on decisions where it is actually right 72% of the time, a threshold of 0.85 gives you false security. Independent benchmarks on JevBench suggest that Jev currently has the best calibration among available options, with open-source implementations closing the gap at a faster rate than expected.

The Current Landscape

The decision model space went from a single proprietary offering to a contested multi-player market in under three weeks. Here is where each option sits as of early October 2026:

ModelArchitectureParametersLatencyCostLicenseDeployment
Jev 1.13 (TypeSafe)Proprietary, parallelUndisclosed70–500ms$0.042/M inputProprietaryCloud API, OpenRouter
Strands Decider 2B (AWS)Qwen3.5-2B + pointer head2B (~1M pointer)~100ms (GPU)Free (self-host)Apache 2.0Local, Bedrock AgentCore
Laya (Convai)ModernBERT-large + decision head421M33ms (GPU)Free (self-host)Apache 2.0Local, Docker, MCP
Kev-4B (Jared Palmer)Qwen3.5-4B + LoRA + pointer4B18ms (H100)Free (self-host)Open weightsLocal server
OpenAI Decisions APIGPT-6 Luna (specialized)Undisclosed~150msProprietaryProprietaryCloud API
OllayaRuntime (bundles Laya, Decider, Kev, others)Various8ms (Laya-multilingual)Free (self-host)Apache 2.0Desktop, Docker, CLI

The architecture split in the open-source landscape is worth understanding, because it produces different practical trade-offs.

  • Laya: uses a bidirectional encoder (ModernBERT-large, 421M parameters) with a trained decision head. Bidirectional encoders read the full context in both directions before producing output, which gives them a strong comprehension at low parameter count. The downside is that Laya’s base checkpoints (without the typed-decisions fine-tune) score only moderately on JevBench.
  • Kev: uses a Qwen3.5 decoder backbone with a rank-16 LoRA adapter and a custom pointer head. The pointer head compares the hidden state at a closing <decide> token with each option’s closing token and returns calibrated probabilities. Because Kev keeps the full autoregressive decoder backbone, it carries the comprehension quality of a generative model while routing output through a pointer rather than a vocabulary distribution. Kev-4B outperforms all three Laya checkpoints on independent 2,394-item evaluations. Kev-27B requires an 80GB GPU or a Mac with 96–128GB unified memory which is closer to a small generative model deployment than a lightweight classifier.
  • Strands Decider 2B: follows Kev’s architectural pattern: a Qwen3.5-2B decoder torso with the language model head removed and replaced by a ~1M parameter pointer head. AWS published the full training recipe and data inventory alongside the weights, making it the most inspectable of the implementations. Independent benchmarks put Strands Decider at 72% routing accuracy on 100-item evals which is lower than Jev’s cloud performance, but competitive with Laya’s base checkpoints. AWS’s documented design intent is for Decider to handle the cases an agent hits reliably (high-frequency, low-ambiguity routing and tool gating) and escalate to an LLM for anything with a confidence below a set threshold. In one head-to-head benchmark against Claude Haiku 4.5, a hybrid pattern — Decider for high-confidence decisions, Haiku only below 0.6 confidence — reached 90% accuracy, compared to 72% for Decider alone.
  • OpenAI’s Decisions API: takes a different approach from all the open models: it routes through a specialized version of GPT-6 Luna rather than a purpose-built decision architecture. The practical implication is that it likely has higher comprehension quality than any of the open models at the cost of proprietary pricing and the constraint that inputs route through OpenAI’s infrastructure. It supports text and image inputs, which none of the open models currently supports.

Where Decision Models Fit in an Agent Pipeline

The twelve use cases that have emerged most consistently across the developer community building with these models in the first weeks of the category are worth mapping explicitly, because the right mental model is not “a decision model does classification” — it is “a decision model handles every bounded choice that currently runs through your LLM unnecessarily.”

Routing and orchestration

  • Model routing: score incoming request complexity and route to the cheapest model that can handle it. A decision model evaluating complexity as low/medium/high with a confidence score can replace a set of hand-written rules or an expensive preliminary LLM call. The compounding savings on a high-volume pipeline are significant, e.g. every request that correctly routes to Deepseek V4-Flash instead of Claude Opus 4.7 saves roughly $24.72/M output tokens.
  • Tool selection: given a description of available tools and the current agent state, which tool should the agent call next? This is exactly a bounded choice from a known option set.
  • Orchestration forking: in a multi-agent system, which agent should handle this subtask? The decision model scores each agent against the current state and returns confidence-weighted assignments

Safety and guardrails

  • Tool call gating: before executing a proposed tool call, verify that the parameters are grounded in what the user actually said. AWS’s documented Strands example catches a weather agent calling a tool before the user specified a city which the decision model flags as premature rather than letting the agent hallucinate a location. This pattern sits between the agent and every tool call and adds sub-100ms overhead.
  • Destructive action classification: is this shell command / database write / file deletion safe to auto-execute, or should it escalate to a human? A decision model with calibrated confidence makes this gate tunable where you can set the threshold based on the cost of a wrong execution in your environment.
  • Content policy: is this user message within scope for this application? Routing out-of-scope requests at the decision layer rather than the LLM layer saves the full LLM call cost on every rejected input.

Evaluation and quality control

  • Completion verification: is the agent’s task actually done, or has it incorrectly concluded? This is one of the most persistent failure modes in agentic coding. The agent reports success when the tests fail or the implementation is incomplete. A decision model evaluating completion at each loop iteration with a confidence threshold adds a lightweight check before the agent exits.
  • Output quality scoring: score the LLM’s last output on relevance, accuracy, or task alignment before passing it downstream. Cheap per-check cost makes this viable at every generation step rather than as a post-hoc review.

Memory and context management

  • Memory retrieval relevance: of these ten retrieved memory chunks, which ones are actually relevant to the current query? A decision model replaces a secondary LLM call for reranking.
  • Context compression gating: has enough new information arrived to warrant updating the agent’s working memory, or can the current context continue? A low-cost judgment that runs continuously without adding significant overhead.
  • Priority classification: in a queue of pending tasks, score each one for urgency and route accordingly.

What these use cases show

The common thread across all of these is that the decision is bounded and repetitive. You know the option set in advance. The right answer does not require generating an explanation. Running a frontier LLM for this is like hiring a senior engineer to answer yes/no questions all day which is technically capable, but not the right tool for the task.

The Benchmark That Emerged Alongside the Category

JevBench, a benchmark for evaluating decision models on routing and classification tasks, appeared alongside Jev and has become the de facto comparison standard across implementations. Independent results from early October 2026 put Jev (the proprietary TypeSafe model) at 63.29 (86.6% public / 36.7% sealed accuracy), with Strands Decider 2B at 0.723 (72.3% accuracy on 231 items), and Laya’s base 421M checkpoint at 30.25 on the same scale.

Two things to note about these numbers. First, the gap between Jev and the open-source implementations is real on hard items, but the base Laya checkpoint is the wrong comparison. The laya-typed-decisions fine-tuned checkpoint scores 0.766 accuracy on its own benchmark and is the one designed for production agent decision tasks. Second, all of these models are weeks old. The open-source implementations are closing the gap faster than expected; the rate of improvement visible in the Kev results (Kev-4B outperforming all Laya checkpoints on a 2,394-item eval) suggests the category will look different in six months.

The honest calibration finding from independent testing: Strands Decider 2B’s 72% standalone accuracy becomes 90% in a hybrid architecture where the LLM handles low-confidence cases. For most production use cases, the right question is not “can this model match Jev?” but “what is the accuracy-cost trade-off for routing n% of decisions through Decider and the remainder through an LLM?”

The Caveats with Decision Models

Decision models solve a real problem, and the category has momentum that is unlikely to reverse. But three limitations are worth knowing before you commit to one in production.

The gap on hard items is real

JevBench’s sealed accuracy scores reveal that open-source implementations perform significantly worse than Jev on genuinely ambiguous or complex decisions. A high-confidence prediction on a clear routing case is not the same as reliable performance on a borderline case. If your application depends on correct decisions at the tails of the distribution the current open-source options are not there yet. The hybrid architecture pattern (decision model for high-confidence cases, LLM fallback for the rest) is the engineering response to this limitation, and it is the pattern AWS explicitly recommends for Strands Decider.

Decision models do not reason

Returning a bounded choice from a predefined set is not the same as understanding why that choice is correct. A decision model that classifies a message as “billing” cannot explain its reasoning, cannot catch edge cases that fall outside its training distribution, and cannot generalize to option sets it has never seen. For applications where the decision requires understanding novel context, generating a brief explanation, or handling options that were not available at training time, a decision model is the wrong tool.

CPU deployment is slow

Strands Decider 2B on CPU takes 4+ seconds per decision which is slower than a fast LLM API call. The latency advantage of decision models is contingent on GPU inference. For local deployments on developer machines or edge environments without GPU acceleration, the latency profile changes substantially. Ollaya’s Laya-multilingual checkpoint is the fastest available at 8ms median on GPU; on CPU, expect that number to increase by 50–100x depending on hardware.

What This Means for Agent Pipeline Design

The emergence of decision models as a distinct layer in the agent stack changes the design pattern for pipelines running at scale. The previous options for agent control flow were: encode the decision in code (rules tables, if/else logic), make an LLM call and parse the output, or use structured outputs with a generative model. Each has costs: rules tables are brittle and cannot handle semantic complexity, LLM calls are expensive and slow, structured outputs still pay the full generation cost and add parsing overhead.

Decision models add a fourth option: a purpose-built judgment layer at sub-200ms latency and near-zero output cost, with calibrated confidence that enables threshold-based automation. The right architecture is not decision models instead of LLMs but it is decision models for the high-frequency bounded choices that do not require generative reasoning, with LLMs reserved for the long-horizon tasks that do.

The practical starting point for most teams is model routing. A decision model that correctly identifies 80% of requests as suitable for a cheap model (V4-Flash, Haiku) and routes the remaining 20% to a frontier model captures most of the cost savings of the category without requiring deep pipeline restructuring. At $0.042/M input tokens for Jev or self-hosted Strands Decider at zero marginal cost, the routing layer pays for itself on the first day of production traffic.

The category is three weeks old. The infrastructure around suggests that decision models are not a product announcement but a new layer in the agent infrastructure stack. The next time your agent makes a bounded choice, the question worth asking is whether that choice needs a language model at all.

item.title: Best Qwen3.8-27B Inference Providers (2026)
item.content:encoded:
Best Qwen3.8-27B Inference Providers (2026)

Published on 2026.10.10 by DeepInfra

Qwen3.8-27B has shifted the landscape of open-weight models. It strikes an exceptional balance between parameter count and reasoning capability: a 27-billion parameter model that is highly capable yet compact. It runs on a single 24GB card at 4-bit quantization, or a single 80GB card at full precision. Finding the right infrastructure to host, scale, or access it via API remains a real decision point. Latency, throughput, and cost can make or break an AI application in production, especially for agentic workflows or high-volume inference.

This guide breaks down the best SaaS tools, API providers, and hosting solutions for Qwen3.8-27B. Whether you need ultra-low latency inference, a massive context window, or cost-effective self-hosting, the breakdown below covers the ecosystem so you can pick the right infrastructure.

Summary: Best Providers by Use Case

Use CaseBest Provider
Best overall API accessDeepInfra, for cost-efficiency and production reliability
Massive context and enterpriseAlibaba Cloud, first-party, with a 1M-token context window
Ultra-low latencyCerebras, wafer-scale hardware at roughly 1,500 tokens per second
Throughput and quick first responseMultiverse Computing, among the fastest traditional API providers
API aggregation and routingOpenRouter, routes across 17 providers with automatic failover
High-volume self-hostingAkash Network, decentralized bare-metal GPUs
Serverless deploymentsRunPod, scale-to-zero endpoints
Managed orchestrationNorthflank, bring-your-own-cloud with managed Kubernetes
Budget-conscious developmentNovita AI, competitive pricing with steep cache discounts

Best Qwen3.8-27B Providers (Deep Dive)

DeepInfra

DeepInfra stands out as the best overall solution for accessing Qwen3.8-27B: a competitive, scalable API that integrates into production environments without the overhead of managing hardware.

  • Input: $0.15 per 1M tokens (current promotional rate; list price $0.20)
  • Output: $1.875 per 1M tokens (current; list price $2.50)
  • Cached input: $0.038 per 1M tokens
  • Blended rate: $0.24 per 1M tokens (7:2:1 cache/input/output ratio), the second-cheapest of the 8 providers Artificial Analysis tracks for this model
  • Context window: 262,144 tokens natively, extensible to 1M via YaRN
  • Features: Function calling, JSON mode, multimodal (image and video) input, prompt caching

DeepInfra is the choice for teams that want reliable, scalable API access to Qwen3.8-27B without self-hosting, at one of the lowest blended rates among tracked providers. Full current rates are on the pricing page, and the API reference covers every available parameter.

Alibaba Cloud

As the official creator and first-party provider of the Qwen model family, Alibaba Cloud offers a managed API service built to handle extreme context lengths natively, useful for enterprise applications that digest massive documents or long chat histories.

  • Input: $0.42 to $0.50 per 1M tokens, depending on tier
  • Output: $3.00 per 1M tokens
  • Context window: Up to 1M tokens by default
  • Token Plan: Alibaba’s broader Model Studio subscription starts at $6/month (early-bird rate). It bundles credit-based access across the model lineup, including Qwen3.8-Max, rather than billing Qwen3.8-27B specifically per token

Alibaba Cloud is the choice for enterprises and developers who want official, first-party access and the full 1M-token context window that some third-party hosts cap lower.

Cerebras

When latency is the top priority, Cerebras is in a league of its own. Its wafer-scale hardware, rather than traditional GPUs, serves Qwen3.8-27B at speeds other providers cannot match. It suits real-time voice agents or multi-step reasoning loops, where every second of wait time compounds.

  • Speed: Approximately 1,500 output tokens per second, per Cerebras’s own published figures
  • Pricing: $0.99 input and $1.49 output per 1M tokens
  • Context window: 128K tokens on paid developer tiers (64K on the free trial)
  • API: OpenAI-compatible, with tool calling and structured outputs

Cerebras added Qwen3.8-27B to its public catalog in September 2026, alongside its existing small, pay-per-token model lineup. It is built for latency-sensitive applications and agentic workflows that need fast token generation, not broad model selection or self-hosting flexibility.

Multiverse Computing

Multiverse Computing is among the fastest traditional API providers tracked for Qwen3.8-27B. For interactive applications where time to first token matters for user experience, it posts some of the lowest latency in the field.

  • Input: $0.40 per 1M tokens
  • Output: $2.00 per 1M tokens
  • Output speed: Around 190 tokens per second in Artificial Analysis benchmarks, among the fastest tracked for this model
  • Latency: 0.66 seconds to first token, the lowest Artificial Analysis records for this model
  • Features: Native support for JSON mode and function calling

Multiverse Computing suits throughput-intensive tasks and interactive applications that need quick first responses, without relying on Cerebras’s specialized hardware.

OpenRouter

OpenRouter is a unified API aggregator that abstracts away the complexity of managing multiple provider endpoints. It routes Qwen3.8-27B requests across its network of hosts to balance price, speed, and uptime.

  • Providers: Routes across 17 different backends serving Qwen3.8-27B, per OpenRouter’s own listing
  • Pricing: Varies by routed backend. OpenRouter’s own default listing shows $0.0248 input and $4.35 output per 1M tokens, and requests can also route to cheaper backends such as DeepInfra
  • Reliability: Built-in failover and load balancing across backends
  • API: OpenAI-compatible drop-in replacement

OpenRouter suits developers who want broad model access, automatic failover, and the ability to route requests dynamically, at the cost of a single predictable price point.

Akash Network

For teams operating at scale, per-token billing eventually becomes a bottleneck. Akash Network runs a decentralized GPU marketplace where developers bid for bare-metal capacity to self-host Qwen3.8-27B, often well below traditional cloud rates.

  • A100 (80GB): Starting around $1.07 per hour on Akash’s marketplace
  • H100 (80GB): Typically in the $1.30 to $2 per hour range, though Akash runs a reverse-auction market, so rates move with provider bids and demand
  • Economics: Fixed hourly costs that can undercut per-token billing at high volumes
  • Control: Full control over data residency and privacy, since inference runs on hardware you rent directly

Akash Network suits high-volume users who want to self-host Qwen3.8-27B to eliminate per-token costs and keep data on infrastructure they control.

RunPod

RunPod bridges the gap between managed APIs and bare-metal hosting with serverless GPU endpoints. Because Qwen3.8-27B is compact enough to fit on consumer-grade cards at lower precision, RunPod lets you deploy it cost-effectively and pay only for active compute time.

  • Hardware: Supports 24GB worker slices, such as RTX 3090, 4090, and 6000 Ada
  • Cold starts: FlashBoot memory snapshotting reduces cold-start latency
  • Billing: Per-second billing for active execution, with scale-to-zero when idle

RunPod suits teams deploying Qwen3.8-27B on serverless infrastructure that want to minimize idle cost without managing their own cluster.

Northflank

Northflank is a cloud platform for production teams that want to self-host Qwen3.8-27B alongside existing microservices. It handles the Kubernetes and GPU orchestration so you can focus on the application.

  • Deployment: Runs Qwen3.8-27B as a GPU-backed service using SGLang or vLLM
  • BYOC: Bring Your Own Cloud support for enterprise environments
  • Scope: Managed Kubernetes and GPU infrastructure alongside application services and databases in one stack

Northflank suits production teams that want to self-host securely without taking on the operational burden of Kubernetes or GPU orchestration themselves.

Novita AI

Novita AI focuses on driving down the cost of inference. For applications with heavy prompt repetition, such as RAG pipelines or document analysis, its caching discount is one of the steepest among tracked providers.

  • Input: $0.42 per 1M tokens
  • Output: $3.00 per 1M tokens
  • Cached input: $0.085 per 1M tokens
  • API: Fully OpenAI-compatible

Novita AI is a strong choice for budget-conscious developers who want reliable, cheap API access to Qwen3.8-27B, particularly when prompt caching applies.

Conclusion and Recommendations

Selecting the right infrastructure for Qwen3.8-27B depends on workload requirements, budget, and engineering resources.

  • Enterprises and massive context: Alibaba Cloud is the clear choice for official support and the full 1M-token context window.
  • Speed and agentic workflows: Cerebras offers the fastest raw token generation, while Multiverse Computing provides the lowest latency among traditional API providers.
  • Self-hosting and high volume: Akash Network offers the cheapest bare-metal compute, RunPod gives scale-to-zero serverless flexibility, and Northflank suits teams that need managed Kubernetes orchestration.
  • Budget and flexibility: Novita AI delivers strong cost savings through prompt caching, and OpenRouter provides dynamic routing across multiple providers.

For a balanced, production-ready default, DeepInfra pairs one of the lowest blended rates among tracked providers with function calling, JSON mode, and multimodal support out of the box. Browse the full model catalogue or the broader Qwen model family to compare options before committing to a provider. Deploy a private endpoint if you need dedicated capacity.

item.title: Qwen3.8-27B: Frontier-Level Vision-Language AI
item.content:encoded:
Qwen3.8-27B: Frontier-Level Vision-Language AI

Published on 2026.10.09 by DeepInfra

Qwen3.8-27B is a 27-billion parameter dense vision-language model built to close the gap between compact deployment and frontier-level performance. It is engineered for complex, multi-step tasks, including coding, professional research, and long-horizon agentic workflows.

The model pairs a native vision encoder with a 262,144-token context window, extensible to 1,000,000 tokens. It reads both text and visual data, from STEM diagrams to hour-scale video. It suits teams building autonomous agents or document intelligence tools that reason over images and long documents in the same request.

Latest Developments and Architecture

Qwen3.8-27B is built on the architectural foundation of the Qwen3.5 series and introduces several changes over its predecessor, Qwen3.6-27B.

Under the hood, it is a 64-layer causal language model with a vision encoder attached, with a hidden dimension of 5,120. The layout mixes linear-attention (Gated DeltaNet) blocks with full-attention (Gated Attention) blocks, and multi-token prediction is trained in to speed up generation.

Flexible thinking control

One of the most significant additions in Qwen3.8 is flexible thinking control, which gives developers granular command over the model’s reasoning process. Thinking mode is on by default and can be disabled per request, or tuned rather than switched off entirely:

  • Reasoning depth: Use the reasoning_effort parameter to align compute resources with task complexity.
  • Thinking persistence: The preserve_thinking parameter retains reasoning context from earlier messages, improving continuity in long-running agentic workflows.

Native multimodal intelligence

Rather than relying on external vision plugins, Qwen3.8-27B has native support for image and video understanding. It processes complex documents and visual data within its 262,144-token native context window.

Performance Benchmarks and Comparative Analysis

Qwen3.8-27B outperforms Qwen3.6-27B and Muse Glimmer-30B across most text and multimodal evaluations, and beats the larger Opus4.6 Max on several agentic and coding benchmarks.

Text and reasoning performance

BenchmarkQwen3.8-27BQwen3.6-27BMuse Glimmer-30BOpus4.6 Max
GPQA Diamond (scientific reasoning)89.287.883.591.3
SWE-bench Pro (agentic coding)61.753.551.253.4
LiveCodeBench v6 (competitive coding)90.383.9N/A88.8
IFBench (instruction following)79.569.177.062.5
CoWorkBench (long-horizon office work)70.761.0N/A68.2

Vision-language performance

BenchmarkQwen3.8-27BQwen3.6-27BMuse Glimmer-30BOpus4.6 Max
OSWorld-Verified (computer use)84.363.965.972.7
MathVision, with reasoning (visual math)94.685.1N/A65.5
OmniDocBench 1.5 (document intelligence)91.189.4N/A86.6
RealWorldQA (perception)85.984.1N/A73.9

Key highlights

  • Agentic execution: The model leads OSWorld-Verified for UI navigation at 84.3. It also ties the strongest result on multimodal tool use, with a Pass@3 of 57.4 on ClawEval-MM.
  • Software engineering: A score of 79.0 on the internal QwenSWEBench is the best in its comparison set, well ahead of Qwen3.6-27B at 49.3 and Opus4.6 Max at 63.8. It marks a substantial jump in handling complex, multi-file codebases.
  • Efficiency: Multi-token prediction is trained into the architecture, which typically improves inference speed by generating more than one token per forward pass.

Getting Started with the API

DeepInfra provides an OpenAI-compatible API to integrate Qwen3.8-27B into your applications.

Authentication

To interact with the API, use your DeepInfra API key in the HTTP headers:

Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_DEEPINFRA_API_KEY>
Content-Type: application/jsoncopy

API endpoint basics

  • Endpoint: https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai/chat/completions
  • Model identifier: Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B

The full parameter reference, including streaming, is on the Qwen3.8-27B API page.

Using cURL

curl https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEEPINFRA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "model": "Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B",
    "messages": [
      {
        "role": "user",
        "content": "Write a Python function to check if a number is prime."
      }
    ]
  }'copy

Using Python

import requests
import os

API_KEY = os.getenv("DEEPINFRA_API_KEY")
url = "https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai/chat/completions"

headers = {
    "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}",
    "Content-Type": "application/json"
}

payload = {
    "model": "Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain the benefits of the Qwen3.8 architecture."}]
}

response = requests.post(url, headers=headers, json=payload)
print(response.json())copy

Advanced Configuration Parameters

Customize the model’s behavior with the following parameters in the JSON payload:

ParameterTypeDescription
modelstringRequired. Set to Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B.
messagesarrayRequired. Supports text, image, and video inputs.
reasoning_effortstring / floatTunes reasoning depth when thinking mode is active.
preserve_thinkingbooleanRetains reasoning context across multi-turn conversations.
response_formatobjectUse {“type”: “json_object”} for structured JSON output.
streambooleanSet to true to receive the response as a token stream.

Pricing and Cost Optimization

DeepInfra prices Qwen3.8-27B per token, with a 25% promotional discount currently applied to the standard tier and a further break on cached input. Cached input already runs 75% below the standard input rate at list price, which matters for repetitive prompts such as reused system messages or tool schemas.
